Location: Zoom
Attendees: Evan Lopez (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ravi Mehta (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Arcadia), Devon Park (Arcadia), Jules Mbatha (Arcadia), Anika Bose (Arcadia)

---- Transcript Body:
[00:00:00] Evan Lopez: Hey everyone thanks for making time. quick intro — i'm Evan from Redwood, with Priya and Ravi on the eng side. uh can we do quick intros?
[00:00:12] Marta Ruiz: Yeah I'm Marta, head of ML at Arcadia. we run risk-scorers and doc summarization for underwriting. sequence distribution skews 32 to 512 tokens depending on doc.
[00:00:28] Jules Mbatha: Jules here, CTO. main ask is keep p95 latency under 300ms for interactive scoring, secure everything; we need tenant separation.
[00:00:38] Devon Park: Devon, infra lead — VPC peering and on-prem options are a hard req. network egress controls, and KMS per tenant if possible.
[00:00:46] Priya Nair: great, thanks. goal today is to propose a prefix/prompt caching approach that maximizes hit rate while preventing cross-tenant leakage and fits your VPC/on-prem requirements. we'll also cover batching/quantization tradeoffs.

[00:01:05] Ravi Mehta: quick state question — are you today using a single prompt template across tenants or many per-client?
[00:01:12] Marta Ruiz: mix — we have shared templates for summarization but each client pins a few custom instructions; so there is a lot of repetition inside a tenant but less cross-tenant commonality.

[00:01:30] Priya Nair: ok that helps. first principle: cache keys must incorporate tenant id + template fingerprint + normalized prompt prefix. we recommend a layered key e.g. tenant|template_hash|prefix_norm|model_variant. that prevents accidental cross-tenant hits.
[00:01:55] Devon Park: when you say normalized prefix, how lossy is normalization? we can't leak PII across cache entries.
[00:02:02] Priya Nair: good question — normalization should strip variable fields and replace with placeholders where possible; for ambiguous regions the safest is to avoid caching at that granularity. we also support encrypted cache namespaces per-tenant when on Redwood Dedicated/Private — so key names are hashed with tenant-specific salt and optional KMS-wrapped keys.
[00:02:30] Evan Lopez: to add — for our Private offering inside a customer's VPC we can mount the cache inside their subnet and optionally use customer-managed KMS so keys never leave their control.

[00:02:48] Jules Mbatha: ok. what's realistic hit rate given our workload?
[00:02:52] Priya Nair: with templated prompts and 70% repeat prefixes within a tenant, we see simulated warm hit rates between 45-65% at the prefix level for windows of 1-6 hours. if you include KV prefix continuation caching (i.e., KV cache for autoregressive tokens), effective token-level savings are higher.
[00:03:17] Marta Ruiz: those are optimistic numbers; our prompts mutate slightly, we do A/B test variants. how do you handle near-duplicate prefixes?
[00:03:26] Ravi Mehta: we implement fuzzy-key buckets — something like normalized edit-distance thresholds and consistent hashing into buckets. bucket keys map to cached continuations; on a miss we fall back to model compute and then populate the bucket if the result is stable. there's a tradeoff there: fuzzier buckets raise hit rate but risk semantic mismatch.
[00:03:52] Devon Park: i want to understand risk — could a prompt from tenant A mutate such that it matches tenant B's cached continuation?
[00:03:59] Priya Nair: not if you include tenant scoping in the key. cross-tenant leakage only happens if tenant id is excluded or misconfigured. we also add an integrity hash over prompt metadata and optional per-tenant salt; keys are HMAC'd so you can't just guess another tenant's key.

[00:04:20] Jules Mbatha: good. what about eviction and TTL strategy? we can't let stale policy decisions persist.
[00:04:26] Priya Nair: recommended multilayer TTLs: short-live prefix cache (30m-2h) for high-churn prompts, medium for common canned responses (6-24h), and longer for static templates (7d+). we also support explicit invalidation APIs so you can purge by template id or tag when you roll model updates.
[00:04:48] Marta Ruiz: and how do you measure correctness/regression when using cached continuations? we can't silently degrade quality.
[00:04:54] Ravi Mehta: we tie cache population to eval hooks — before caching a continuation we run lightweight heuristics (e.g., length, policy checks) and optional re-eval on a held-out probe set. also Redwood Optimize can surface regression alerts if cached outputs diverge after model rollouts.

[00:05:18] Anika Bose: on the subject of quantization — we're worried that 4-bit quantized models will change token distributions and make cached continuations invalid faster. does Redwood handle quantization-specific cache versioning?
[00:05:30] Priya Nair: yes, include model_variant (quantization level and kernel profile) in the cache key. if you roll from fp16 to an int4 profile we will separate namespaces; we also recommend warming the cache with a warm-up batch when deploying a quantized variant.

[00:05:48] Devon Park: performance numbers — what latency/throughput differences should we expect when relying on prefix cache hits vs full generation?
[00:05:55] Ravi Mehta: on our benchmark suite, a token-level cache hit can cut per-request tail latency by 40-70% depending on sequence length and model. for example for a 256-token request with an avg 60-token prefix cached, p95 drops from ~420ms to ~180ms on same hardware. throughput improves because less GPU attention work is required, though you still pay for small decode steps.
[00:06:21] Marta Ruiz: that's promising. can we see those numbers on our exact model and quantization?
[00:06:25] Priya Nair: yes — next step we propose a 48-72 hour benchmark in your VPC/dedicated namespace with your prompt set and a mix of quant variants. we'll provide the benchmark harness.

[00:06:41] Jules Mbatha: security checklist please — SOC2, SSO, audit logs, per-tenant KMS, and ability to show exact cache keys and operations during incident investigation.
[00:06:50] Evan Lopez: we'll send the SOC2 pack and a cache-audit example. audit logs include cache gets/puts and invalidation events with masked prompt fingerprints (we never store raw PII in logs unless customer opts in).

[00:07:02] Devon Park: about on-prem — does oak run in air-gapped mode? how does the cache sync work?
[00:07:09] Priya Nair: for on-prem we provide an appliance that runs the runtime and KV cache locally. you can choose: local-only cache (no external sync) or optional cross-site replication across your colo via our replication protocol. replication is encrypted and uses customer-managed TLS certs.

[00:07:25] Marta Ruiz: replication brings complexity for compliance; we prefer local-only for now.
[00:07:29] Ravi Mehta: local-only is fine — it actually simplifies tenant isolation. all keys are namespaced per-tenant and we can run with customer KMS so the cache encryption keys are not visible to Redwood.

[00:07:40] Priya Nair: one more practical pattern: prefetching. if you can identify next-step prompts deterministically (e.g., known convo flows), Redwood can prewarm the KV cache during low load windows. prefetching is a big win for p95.
[00:07:54] Anika Bose: any danger in prefetching wrong continuations and polluting cache?
[00:07:58] Priya Nair: we prefetch into a separate warm-bucket and only promote to hot cache after validation, or keep TTL short for prefetched entries. also you can mark flows as eligible for prefetch via API.

[00:08:15] Jules Mbatha: what about cost levers — batching and quantization?
[00:08:19] Ravi Mehta: batching increases throughput but also increases latency variability; we have continuous batching that tries to keep p95 SLOs by capping batch wait time and using smaller batches for low latency customers. quantization reduces GPU memory & increases throughput but can slightly reduce output quality; use evaluation thresholds to decide. caching often gives the best unit-cost wins because it reduces total tokens generated.

[00:08:44] Marta Ruiz: practical question — how do we design cache-key churn controls for AB tests? we run many small experiments that change prompt wording often.
[00:08:53] Priya Nair: tag keys with experiment id and provide a naming convention for ephemeral experiments. TTLs can be very short for experiment-tagged entries and you can bulk purge experiment tags post-run. also consider using a hash of normalized prompt minus experiment tokens to retain some shared cache across experiments.

[00:09:12] Devon Park: okay, i'd like to see a concrete cache key schema doc and the corresponding invalidation API.
[00:09:17] Evan Lopez: Priya will produce that.

[00:09:22] Priya Nair: we'll also include sample HMAC salted key examples, a hashed key naming convention, and example CLI commands to purge by template id or tag.

[00:09:35] Marta Ruiz: can Redwood's Optimize tool suggest TTLs and bucket sizes based on our telemetry?
[00:09:40] Ravi Mehta: yes — Redwood Optimize analyzes request traces, sequence lengths, and repetition rates to suggest TTL bins, bucket thresholds, and even whether a particular template is worth caching. it can output a config you can apply to your tenant namespace.

[00:09:57] Anika Bose: are there any gotchas for multi-region deployments? we have users across NA and EU.
[00:10:03] Priya Nair: prefer region-local caches to minimize cross-region egress and latency. for shared state we recommend asynchronous replication with conflict resolution by last-write or by tag precedence. also mind data residency: keep EU tenant data in EU-local cache nodes.

[00:10:20] Jules Mbatha: last bit — SLA/rollback behavior when a model rollout causes quality regression on cached outputs. can we auto-disable caching during rollout?
[00:10:29] Priya Nair: yes, rollouts can be configured to disable cache population for the new model until a validation window passes; we also support canary traffic that goes uncached or uses separate cache namespaces. automatic rollback triggers can be based on eval probes that check cached output metrics.

[00:10:48] Evan Lopez: great — let's recap concrete next steps.
[00:10:51] Evan Lopez: Redwood will send the security pack, cache-key schema doc, and benchmark harness. we'll set up a pilot namespace in your VPC (local-only cache) and run 48-72h with your prompts. you're going to export 5k sample prompts and mark flows eligible for prefetch. we'll reconvene after pilot results.
[00:11:12] Marta Ruiz: sounds good. who owns kickoff scheduling?
[00:11:15] Evan Lopez: i'll own scheduling; expect a calendar invite after i share the security docs.

[00:11:22] Jules Mbatha: one procedural note — we need formal SSO and compliance review before any on-prem appliance install.
[00:11:28] Evan Lopez: understood. we'll loop in security & compliance.

[00:11:32] Devon Park: thanks everyone.
[00:11:35] (call continues with some screen-sharing of a rough cache key doc and a short demo of the audit events UI; some audio dropouts between 00:34:10-00:35:05 causing minor transcription errors)

[00:34:10] Priya Nair: ...so here's an example key: HMAC( tenant_salt | template_v1 | norm_prefix | model:q4_kv ) -> base64-key. when you call cache:get we return masked fingerprint and a small metadata object: prefix_length, ttl_remaining, created_at, and a stable content_hash. you can opt in to full raw prefix logging but it's disabled by default.
[00:34:35] Marta Ruiz: is the metadata enough for forensic audits?
[00:34:38] Ravi Mehta: yes, metadata plus HMAC key lineage helps reconstruct events without exposing raw PII.

[00:50:00] Evan Lopez: closing notes — we'll prepare the docs and benchmark harness; pilot kickoff tentative 2025-11-12.
[00:50:12] Jules Mbatha: thanks all.
